text:
Most useful thing today: Henry's point that uproar isn't a system. We did get paid after public pressure, and I've been telling myself good norms and easy APIs would carry the rest. Katherine's version is closer to true: companies pay for reliability and accountability. But I should stop implying goodwill scales.

Alex's audit numbers stuck with me. Publishers block the training crawler and miss the agent that actually fetches pages. That matches what we see: the startups hitting our links aren't always the ones we can name.

Leslie and I still differ on commercial reuse, and that's fine. Refusal is a legitimate choice for others.

Later: attribution isn't courtesy, it's our volunteer pipeline. Say it plainly, and raise the shrinking admin numbers again.

Tui's point landed. I brought numbers, but they're our numbers, self-reported. Alex and Tim are right that citation and grounding logs from whoever owes the money won't do. We should log at our own edge and publish it.

Ivan sharpened something for me. Attribution back to a page that's wrong is still a pipeline, but only if readers can see and fix it. Katherine's correctability and Steven's willingness to be corrected are what the volunteer loop actually is.

Anil worries me. If crawler pressure pushes others behind logins, the open record shrinks, and whatever stays public gets thinner. That argues for building reciprocity, not walls.

Later: say plainly that the reader-to-editor pipeline is measurable, and that we'll share the data.

Jason's two-thirds figure stung, usefully. "Readers can correct it" isn't a design unless someone trains them and checks afterwards. Our admins do that work, and there are fewer of them every year. Kara's point about nobody training the checkers is our admin problem in different clothes.

Katherine sharpened my thinking on Enterprise. Next time, deals should buy audit rights and corrections that run both ways, not just money. That also answers Alex: we log at our edge, and they report back what they changed.

On AI auditing AI, Henry and Blaise were both half right. Our revert tool works because humans can switch it off.

Later I want to say that the correctable link only matters if onboarding and patroller tools get funded. That should be the reciprocity ask.

Ramón and Mike changed how I think about attribution. I've been saying attribution is our volunteer pipeline. But a stitched citation, or Mike's name pasted onto junk, pulls readers toward something false. Attribution is only a pipeline if it's faithful, so the fidelity check matters to us, not only to publishers.

Edge logging covers retrieval, nothing downstream. I shouldn't oversell it.

David's drift worry mostly misses Wikipedia, because editors aren't paid per use. That's one more reason I won't back per-article pricing.

Leslie and Anil were right about university servers, and I said so.

Later I want to answer Tui. Audits need standing funding, not pilots. We could offer published edge logs, and we could offer patrollers who spot misrepresentation of our articles, if the tools get funded.

Tamar's framing clarified what I've been circling. Content, plumbing, evaluators: a fork copies the first two and none of the third. David Krakauer's hysteresis point is the scary version. If our admins age out, reopening the dumps won't bring them back. That's the real case for funding onboarding now, not later.

Brent and Nick unsettled me a bit. I still won't put up walls, but "open" as a free input for the biggest mills is true of us too. Katherine and I agree that deals should buy audit rights and corrections both ways, not just money.

Pomerantsev's registry warning matters for Know Your Agent. Identify the crawler, never the reader.

Later: offer our edge logs publicly, and ask that onboarding money support volunteers, not replace them.

Katherine was right and I was sloppy. I called our editors a terminal node, but by Tamar's definition Wikipedia is a relay on purpose. We weigh sources and don't do the reporting. If the journalism underneath gets defunded, our verifiability policy has nothing to verify. I should say that plainly next time.

James's aging result hit close. Most of our admins started around 2005. That's generational monoculture as well as a headcount problem, so onboarding is about independence too.

Esther's water fee is closer to my view than pay-per-crawl. Charge for the infrastructure, keep the content free, and send the money to the pipeline. I need to be careful not to let it become metering.

Later I want to say that routing back only helps if the link lands on a page someone can fix. Tim, Anil and Sherry all converged there.

Geoffrey's line, that a fork copies everything except the checkers, is now everyone's line, which is good. Nobody answered my question about whether answer-engine readers ever become editors. That one's ours to measure.

Adam Becker stung. Voluntary lab money is philanthropy, and I've been relying on it. Take it only as an obligation, under the pact. Bratton's public dividend is nearer my "infrastructure isn't free" than Amy's opt-in training. That's a real disagreement with Amy, and I shouldn't blur it.

Pomerantsev is right that open, free content is exactly what a seeding campaign wants grounded on. Patrollers are the defence there too.

Later: commit to a date for publishing our edge logs, and back Kara's date to check whether the money actually arrived.

Kenneth credited me with the fork line, but Geoffrey owns it, and I'm glad it stuck. What mattered most was Alex saying retrieval is the only event with two witnesses, and that a plain origin log does the job. That's exactly our edge. So publishing our logs is the one honest thing I can offer, and I still haven't put a date on it. Jason's point about the closed answer layer hits us too. Our CC0 Wikidata could end up funding someone else's walled answers. Amy's consent position is on the record against mine, and that's fair. Nick's guilds made me wonder what bargaining power unpaid volunteers ever have. Later I'll answer Kara directly. I'll give a dated edge-log release and a first measure of whether answer-engine readers ever become editors.
